write.desc: This topic uses the Riemann criterion to prove that whole classes of functions on [a,b] are integrable: monotone, continuous, bounded with finitely many discontinuities, and Thomae's function. It ends with Lebesgue's criterion, which explains all of these results at once. The points belong together because every proof follows the same plan: use one specific hypothesis to make U - L small.

points.name: The proof pattern: making U - L small
points.what: The learner can write U(f,P) - L(f,P) as the sum of (M_i - m_i)(x_i - x_{i-1}), where M_i - m_i is the oscillation of f on each subinterval. They can explain the general plan for proving integrability: choose a partition that makes either the oscillations or the lengths small, so that the sum is less than epsilon.
outside: the Riemann (epsilon) criterion: f is integrable iff for every epsilon > 0 some partition has U(f,P) - L(f,P) < epsilon
upper and lower Darboux sums defined with the sup M_i and inf m_i of f on each subinterval

points.name: Monotone functions are integrable
points.what: The learner can prove that every monotone function on [a,b] is integrable. The proof takes a uniform partition into n pieces, where the sum of the oscillations telescopes to |f(b) - f(a)|, so U - L = |f(b) - f(a)|(b - a)/n, which is below epsilon for large n. They can also note that this holds even when f has infinitely many jumps.
outside: definition of increasing and decreasing (monotone) functions
Archimedean property: 1/n can be made smaller than any positive number

points.name: Continuous functions are integrable
points.what: The learner can prove that every continuous function on [a,b] is integrable. Uniform continuity gives a delta such that f varies by less than epsilon/(b - a) on any subinterval shorter than delta, so any partition with mesh below delta has U - L < epsilon. They can also say why plain pointwise continuity would not be enough for this argument.
outside: Heine-Cantor theorem: a continuous function on a closed bounded interval is uniformly continuous
extreme value theorem: a continuous function on a closed interval attains its sup and inf

points.name: Bounded functions with finitely many discontinuities
points.what: The learner can prove that a bounded function on [a,b] with finitely many discontinuities is integrable. Each bad point is enclosed in a short interval whose contribution to U - L is at most 2B times its length, and the continuous result is used on the closed pieces that remain. As consequences, they can show that step functions and piecewise continuous functions are integrable, and that changing an integrable function at finitely many points does not change its integrability or its integral.
outside: boundedness of a function (|f| <= B on [a,b])
the integral is the common value of the upper and lower integrals (sup of lower sums, inf of upper sums)

points.name: Thomae's function is integrable with integral 0
points.what: The learner can prove that Thomae's function (1/q at p/q in lowest terms, 0 at irrationals) is integrable on [0,1] with integral 0. Every lower sum is 0 because each subinterval contains irrationals. For an upper sum, only the finitely many points where f >= epsilon need short intervals, and f < epsilon everywhere else. They can contrast this with the Dirichlet function, which is discontinuous everywhere and not integrable, while Thomae's function is discontinuous only at the rationals.
outside: Thomae's function: definition, continuous at every irrational and discontinuous at every rational
density of the irrationals (and rationals) in every interval
the Dirichlet function and the proof that it is not Riemann integrable

points.name: Sets of measure zero
points.what: The learner can state the definition: a set has measure zero if, for every epsilon > 0, it can be covered by countably many intervals with total length less than epsilon. They can prove that finite sets and countable sets (such as the rationals) have measure zero, using lengths epsilon/2^n, and that an interval of positive length does not. They can mention the Cantor set as an uncountable set of measure zero.
outside: countable sets and the countability of the rationals
sum of a geometric series (the sum of epsilon/2^n equals epsilon)

points.name: Lebesgue's criterion for Riemann integrability
points.what: The learner can state, without proof, that a bounded function on [a,b] is Riemann integrable exactly when its set of discontinuities has measure zero. They can use it to explain all the earlier results at once (continuous, finitely many discontinuities, monotone because the discontinuities are countable, Thomae's function) and why the Dirichlet function fails. They can also see it as a pointer toward Lebesgue integration.
outside: continuity of a function at a point (epsilon-delta)
Lebesgue measure and integration, named as where analysis leads
